simple: an arrow that says "this far, in this direction", written as a short list of numbers.
analogy: one robot move on the kitchen floor: so many tiles towards the window, so many away from the door.
precise: an element of the space ℝn, written as an ordered list of n real numbers (v1, …, vn); in 2D and 3D it can be drawn as an arrow whose shift along each axis is one of the numbers. Not the same thing as the C++ container std::vector (KID102 F0-35), which is a resizable list of any type.
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-47 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one of the numbers inside a vector.
analogy: the "towards the window" count, or the "away from the door" count.
precise: the i-th entry vi of a vector v; in 2D the components are usually called x and y, in 3D x, y and z.
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an ordinary single number, used to stretch or shrink a vector.
analogy: "do that move twice as far".
precise: a real number k; multiplying a vector by k multiplies every component by k.
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-47 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the arrow from a fixed starting point (the origin) to a place.
analogy: "the toy is 3 tiles towards the window and 5 tiles away from the door".
precise: the vector from the origin O to a point P; its components are P's coordinates (F0-18).
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a move from one place to another, without caring where it started.
analogy: "3 tiles towards the window", which means the same move from any tile.
precise: the vector B − A that takes point A to point B.
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a mix of vectors, each one stretched by its own number, then added.
analogy: "2 big steps east plus 3 big steps north".
precise: a sum a1v1 + a2v2 + … + amvm with scalars ai and vectors vi.
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-47 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the one-unit arrows along each axis that every other vector is built from.
analogy: "one tile towards the window" and "one tile away from the door".
precise: in ℝ3, ex = (1, 0, 0), ey = (0, 1, 0), ez = (0, 0, 1); every vector is exactly one linear combination of them, and the coefficients are its components.
source: D1 of F0-47 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-47 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long the arrow is.
analogy: measuring a move on the kitchen floor with a tape measure, straight from tail to tip.
precise: |v| = √(v1² + … + vn²), the Euclidean norm; for (3, 4) it is 5.
source: D1 of F0-48 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-48 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an arrow of length exactly 1 that only says "which way".
analogy: pointing your finger in a direction without saying how far.
precise: a vector u with |u| = 1; for any non-zero v, v / |v| is the unit vector in v's direction (normalising). The zero vector has no direction and cannot be normalised.
source: D1 of F0-48 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: multiply matching numbers of two vectors and add the results; the answer is one number.
analogy: the shadow of one arrow on the line of the other, times that other arrow's length.
precise: u · v = u1v1 + … + unvn = |u| |v| cos θ, where θ is the angle between u and v. Also called the scalar product or inner product.
source: D1 of F0-48 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-48 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: at right angles.
analogy: the broom held upright, with no shadow along the floor line.
precise: two vectors are orthogonal when u · v = 0.
source: D1 of F0-48 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-48 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of an arrow that goes along a chosen direction.
analogy: the shadow on the floor line.
precise: for a unit vector d, the scalar projection of v on d is v · d, and the vector projection is (v · d) d; the rest, v − (v · d) d, is orthogonal to d.
source: D1 of F0-48 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-48 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the unit of angle that maths libraries use; a half turn is π radians.
analogy: measuring a turn by how far a point one metre from the centre travels around the circle.
precise: the angle that cuts an arc equal to the radius; 180° = π rad, so 1 rad ≈ 57.2958°. The C++ functions std::cos and std::acos use radians.
source: D1 of F0-48 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B3 of F0-48 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20; registry 4.1)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rectangular table of numbers.
analogy: the recipe card: ingredients down the side, dishes across the top.
precise: an m × n matrix A is an array of m rows and n columns of numbers; its entry in row r and column c is written arc (or A(r, c)).
source: D1 of F0-49 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-49 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one number in the table.
analogy: one box on the recipe card, such as "milk for one cake".
precise: arc, identified by its row index r and column index c. This course numbers rows and columns from 0, as C++ does; many textbooks number from 1 (a11 is the top-left entry there).
source: D1 of F0-49 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many rows and how many columns.
analogy: 3 ingredients by 2 dishes.
precise: the pair m × n, rows first; a 3 × 2 matrix has 6 entries.
source: D1 of F0-49 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: using a table to turn one list of numbers into another.
analogy: batches of each dish in, shopping list out.
precise: for an m × n matrix A and a vector x with n components, Ax is the vector with m components whose entry r is the dot product of row r of A with x; equivalently Ax = x0(column 0) + … + xn−1(column n−1).
source: D1 of F0-49 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-49 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rule that moves every arrow of the plane (or space) so that straight lines stay straight and the origin stays put.
analogy: the recipe card does the same thing to any order: double the order, double the shopping.
precise: a function T with T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(kv) = kT(v); every such T from ℝn to ℝm is "multiply by some m × n matrix".
source: D1 of F0-49 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-49 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: storing a table in memory one row after another.
analogy: reading the recipe card line by line, left to right.
precise: the layout that places entry (r, c) of an m × n matrix at index r × n + c of a one-dimensional array; column-major order places it at c × m + r instead.
source: D1 of F0-49 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: combining two tables into a third, where each box of the answer is "a row of the first times a column of the second".
analogy: recipe card times weekend plan gives ingredients per day.
precise: for A of shape m × k and B of shape k × n, C = AB is m × n with cij = Σp aip bpj (p from 0 to k − 1), the dot product of row i of A and column j of B.
source: D1 of F0-50 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-50 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the size that must match for two matrices to be multiplied.
analogy: the plan must list the same dishes that the recipe card has columns for.
precise: in (m × k)(k × n) the shared k; it disappears from the result's shape m × n.
source: D1 of F0-50 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: swapping the order changes the answer.
analogy: putting on socks then shoes is not shoes then socks.
precise: in general AB ≠ BA; for non-square shapes one of the two may not even be defined.
source: D1 of F0-50 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-50 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the standard name for "multiply two big matrices" in numerical software.
analogy: the whole kitchen planning a whole month.
precise: the general matrix–matrix multiply routine of numerical libraries; in the BLAS interface it also scales and adds, C = αAB + βC; SGEMM is its single-precision form (SP302 F2-56, CU302).
source: D1 of F0-50 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B3 of F0-50 (Kazushige Goto, Robert van de Geijn, "Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one "multiply two numbers and add to a running total" step.
analogy: one line of Lina's sums, such as "100 × 3 added to the flour total".
precise: the unit of work of a matrix product; C = AB with shapes (m × k)(k × n) needs m·n·k multiply-adds, usually counted as 2mnk floating-point operations (flops).
source: D1 of F0-50 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small square piece of a big matrix.
analogy: working on one corner of a big table of numbers at a time.
precise: a submatrix; matrices cut into tiles multiply like matrices of numbers, with tile products in place of number products, which is the basis of cache and GPU tiling (SP302 F2-52, CU302 F6-22).
source: D1 of F0-50 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-50 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the matrix that leaves every vector as it is.
analogy: a recipe step that says "leave it as it is".
precise: the n × n matrix I with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere; IA = A and AI = A whenever the shapes fit, and Ix = x.
source: D1 of F0-51 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-51 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the same table with rows turned into columns.
analogy: flipping the recipe card over its diagonal, so dishes run down the side and ingredients across the top.
precise: for an m × n matrix A, AT is the n × m matrix with (AT)ij = aji. A matrix with AT = A is symmetric.
source: D1 of F0-51 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-51 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one number that says how much a matrix scales areas, and whether it flips them.
analogy: how many floor tiles one tile becomes after the robot's distortion.
precise: for [[a, b], [c, d]], det = ad − bc; |det| is the area of the image of the unit square, and det = 0 exactly when the matrix has no inverse.
source: D1 of F0-51 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-51 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the matrix that undoes another one.
analogy: taking off what you put on.
precise: for a square matrix A, the matrix A−1 with A A−1 = A−1A = I, if it exists; for 2 × 2, A−1 = (1 / det) [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
source: D1 of F0-51 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-51 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a matrix that cannot be undone.
analogy: a squashed map: two different floor tiles land on the same spot, so you cannot tell which one it was.
precise: a square matrix with determinant 0; it sends some non-zero vector to the zero vector and has no inverse. A matrix that has an inverse is called invertible (or non-singular).
source: D1 of F0-51 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-51 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a square matrix whose transpose undoes it.
analogy: a turn of the whole floor, which you undo by turning back.
precise: a square Q with QTQ = I, so Q−1 = QT; its columns are unit vectors at right angles to each other. Rotation matrices (F0-52) are orthogonal.
source: D1 of F0-51 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-51 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: turning everything around a fixed point without stretching or bending it.
analogy: turning the squared paper about the pin.
precise: a linear transformation that keeps lengths and angles and does not mirror; its matrix R satisfies RTR = I and det R = +1.
source: D1 of F0-52 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-52 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra"); B2 of F0-52 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far up you are after walking one step along a direction at angle θ.
analogy: the height of a point on the rim of a turning plate of radius 1.
precise: for the point at angle θ on the circle of radius 1 around the origin, measured anticlockwise from the positive x axis, the point is (cos θ, sin θ); so sin 0° = 0, sin 30° = 0.5, sin 90° = 1.
source: D1 of F0-52 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the 2 × 2 table that turns points by an angle θ.
analogy: the rule for where every dot on the paper goes after the turn.
precise: R(θ) = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], turning anticlockwise by θ for positive θ when x points right and y points up.
source: D1 of F0-52 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-52 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way to tell which turning direction counts as positive in 3D.
analogy: curl the fingers of your right hand around an axis with your thumb along it: the fingers show the positive turn.
precise: in a right-handed coordinate system (x × y = z), a positive rotation about an axis turns x towards y about z, y towards z about x, and z towards x about y.
source: D1 of F0-52 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-52 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the 3 × 3 table that turns points in space.
analogy: turning a whole toy model in your hands.
precise: a 3 × 3 matrix R with RTR = I and det R = +1; the set of all of them is called SO(3), the special orthogonal group. Its columns are the turned x, y and z axes.
source: D1 of F0-52 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-52 (Gilbert Strang, "Introduction to Linear Algebra"); B2 of F0-52 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: which way something points on the floor, as one angle.
analogy: the angle on Kenji's protractor.
precise: for a direction (x, y), the angle atan2(y, x) measured anticlockwise from the x axis, between −180° and 180°; std::atan2 computes it in radians and uses the signs of both arguments to choose the quadrant.
source: D1 of F0-52 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B3 of F0-52 (ISO/IEC 14882, the C++ standard (working draft for C++20)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a starting point and a set of directions from which you measure positions.
analogy: "from the kitchen door: forward and left" versus "from where Kenji stands: in front of him and to his left".
precise: an origin point together with orthonormal axes (right-handed in this course); the coordinates of a point in a frame are its components along those axes measured from that origin.
source: D1 of F0-53 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-53 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the frame fixed to the room or the ground, which does not move.
analogy: the kitchen door and its "forward, left".
precise: a frame W chosen as the fixed reference in which maps, goals and poses are expressed.
source: D1 of F0-53 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-53 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the frame attached to the robot, which moves and turns with it.
analogy: Kenji's "in front of me, to my left".
precise: a frame B with its origin at a chosen point on the robot and its axes fixed to the robot's body; in this course xB points forward and yB to the robot's left.
source: D1 of F0-53 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-53 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: where a robot is and which way it faces.
analogy: "Kenji is three steps in and one to the left, facing the window".
precise: the position t = (x, y) of the body frame's origin and its heading θ (the angle from xW to xB), both expressed in the world frame; together they define the transform from B to W.
source: D1 of F0-53 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-53 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the recipe for turning coordinates in one frame into coordinates in another.
analogy: Amara's rule for turning Kenji's "two steps in front" into her own directions.
precise: the map pW = RWB pB + tWB, where the columns of RWB are B's axes written in W and tWB is B's origin written in W; it keeps distances and angles.
source: D1 of F0-53 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-53 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "which way" and "how far" from the robot to something it senses.
analogy: "60° to my right, two steps away".
precise: for a point pB in the body frame, range = |pB| and bearing = atan2(yB, xB); conversely pB = (range · cos bearing, range · sin bearing).
source: D1 of F0-53 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a point written with one extra number at the end, a 1.
analogy: a parcel label with an extra tick box saying "this is a place, not a direction".
precise: the 2D point (x, y) is written (x, y, 1) and the 3D point (x, y, z) is written (x, y, z, 1); the extra component w lets a single matrix product perform both a rotation and a translation.
source: D1 of F0-54 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-54 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one matrix that holds both a turn and a shift.
analogy: one complete instruction, "from the fridge, turn left and walk two steps".
precise: the (n+1) × (n+1) matrix T = [R t; 0 1], with an n × n rotation R, an n-vector t, and a bottom row of zeros followed by 1; T(p, 1) = (Rp + t, 1). For n = 3 it is a 4 × 4 matrix.
source: D1 of F0-54 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-54 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: following several frame changes in a row by multiplying their matrices.
analogy: "drawer in cupboard, cupboard next to fridge" combined into "from the fridge, here is the spoon".
precise: if TAB maps B coordinates to A coordinates and TBC maps C to B, then TAC = TABTBC; the inner letters must match, and the product does not commute (F0-50).
source: D1 of F0-54 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-54 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the transform that undoes another, going back the opposite way.
analogy: the directions from the spoon back to the fridge.
precise: for T = [R t; 0 1], T−1 = [RT −RTt; 0 1], so TBA = TAB−1.
source: D1 of F0-54 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an arrow that says which way, not where.
analogy: "towards the window" is the same instruction from anywhere in the room.
precise: a vector written with w = 0, such as (x, y, 0); a homogeneous transform rotates it and ignores the shift, because the shift column is multiplied by 0. Displacements (F0-47), velocities and axes are directions.
source: D1 of F0-54 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the family tree of all the frames on a robot, each one attached to a parent.
analogy: spoon in drawer, drawer in cupboard, cupboard in kitchen.
precise: a tree whose nodes are frames and whose edges are transforms; the transform between any two frames is the product of the transforms along the path between them, inverting edges that are walked backwards.
source: D1 of F0-54 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-54 (Kevin M. Lynch and Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: which way a drone or robot is tilted and turned, ignoring where it is.
analogy: how the potato is turned on its skewer, not where it lies on the table.
precise: the orientation of the body frame relative to the world frame, RWB (F0-53), represented by a rotation matrix, a unit quaternion or a set of angles.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B4 of F0-55 (Randal W. Beard and Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number made of four parts, one plain number and three that act like a vector.
analogy: the skewer's direction (three parts) plus how much it is twisted (one part).
precise: q = w + xi + yj + zk, written (w, x, y, z) in this course, with i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B5 of F0-55 (Joan Solà, "Quaternion kinematics for the error-state Kalman filter") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a quaternion of length 1, the kind that describes a rotation.
analogy: a skewer twist written down in a standard size.
precise: q with w² + x² + y² + z² = 1; the rotation by α about the unit axis n is q = (cos(α/2), n sin(α/2)), and q and −q give the same rotation.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rule for multiplying two quaternions; it combines two rotations into one.
analogy: two twists of the skewer, one after the other, replaced by one twist.
precise: (aw, a)(bw, b) = (awbw − a·b, awb + bwa + a × b); not commutative; q2q1 means "q1 first, then q2" in this course's convention.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B5 of F0-55 (Joan Solà, "Quaternion kinematics for the error-state Kalman filter") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the quaternion with its vector part negated; for a unit quaternion, the opposite rotation.
analogy: the same skewer, twisted back.
precise: q* = (w, −x, −y, −z); q q* = (|q|², 0, 0, 0), so for a unit quaternion q* = q−1, playing the role RT plays for matrices (F0-51).
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: three angles, turn left-right, tip nose up-down, roll side to side, that describe an attitude.
analogy: Amara's "turn, tip, roll" instructions.
precise: in this chapter, R = Rz(yaw) Ry(pitch) Rx(roll); other orders and axis choices exist and must be stated.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B4 of F0-55 (Randal W. Beard and Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the pose at which two of the three angles do the same thing, so one direction of turning cannot be expressed.
analogy: the potato tipped straight up, where "turn" and "roll" coincide.
precise: for yaw–pitch–roll at pitch ±90°, the matrix depends only on yaw ∓ roll; the angles cannot be recovered uniquely and small attitude changes can need large angle changes.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: dividing a quaternion by its length so it is exactly length 1 again.
analogy: rescaling a slightly stretched skewer drawing back to standard size.
precise: q ← q / |q|, applied after each update to undo rounding and integration errors that change |q|.
source: D1 of F0-55 (definitions and arithmetic in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
